title: Technical deep dive - Observability & OpenTelemetry token metrics
summary: Deep technical session on integrating OpenTelemetry into Redwood runtime for token-level metrics, tracing, and dashboards. Discussed per-token latency breakdown, KV cache visibility, batching impacts, quantization effects, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed on pilot benchmark and shared dashboards/template OTEL instrumentation guide.
topics: KV cache hit/miss metrics and visibility
Batching behavior and queue/wait time breakdown
Quantization tradeoffs on latency vs quality
VPC / on-prem telemetry and security considerations

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-08
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Atlas - Platform), Priya Menon (Atlas - SRE), Ethan Brooks (Atlas - ML)

Summary (auto): Deep dive on OpenTelemetry integration, what token-level metrics we can expose, and how to build dashboards that show batching and KV cache behavior. Action items captured at end.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you all making time. Quick intro - I'm Ava, AE at Redwood, and Samir is our systems SE who owns the runtime tracing work.
[00:12] Samir Patel: Hi all, thanks. I'll jump into more of the instrumentation details; happy to field infra questions.
[00:18] Jordan Lee: Hey, Jordan here. We're looking to get per-token visibility into latency and understand where our tail is coming from, especially since we saw p99 spikes during peak.
[00:28] Priya Menon: Priya - from SRE. Also concerned about sending telemetry from our VPC to hosted endpoints; need to validate encryption and auditing.
[00:35] Ava Chen: Totally, we'll cover VPC/on-prem OTLP options and encryption. Quick agenda - what to instrument, OpenTelemetry exporters, recommended labels, sampling, dashboards, and a pilot plan.
[00:45] Samir Patel: To start, at the runtime we emit both metrics and spans. Metrics for aggregates - token_count, tokens_per_request, decode_time_total - and spans for per-request and optionally per-token if you enable high-resolution tracing.
[00:58] Ethan Brooks: When you say 'per-token spans', what's the overhead? We worry about OOM or CPU overhead on host.
[01:06] Samir Patel: Good question. Per-token spans are high-cardinality and higher throughput; we recommend them for short pilot windows. Overhead depends on exporter and sampling. If you stream OTLP over gRPC with batching and use async exporters, the CPU overhead is modest but you'll see network egress. For production, we usually surface token-level metrics aggregated into histograms and provide sampled per-token traces for tail analysis.
[01:34] Jordan Lee: Can you show the typical labels we'd attach? We need to know if we'll hit cardinality limits in our telemetry backend.
[01:42] Samir Patel: Typical labels: request_id, model_variant, shard_id, batch_size, prompt_id (hashed), kv_cache_hit boolean, quant_profile (int8, fp16), region, deployment_id. We strongly recommend hashing prompt text to avoid PII in labels. Also avoid unbounded user IDs as labels.
[02:06] Priya Menon: About KV cache - we need hit/miss rates broken down by prefix length and by shard, and ideally the latency saving per hit. Does Redwood expose that?
[02:16] Samir Patel: Yes, we emit kv_cache_hits_total and kv_cache_misses_total per-shard, and a kv_cache_hit_latency_seconds histogram that tracks the delta in decode time when cache hits occur. There's also a cached_prefix_length summary metric we can emit. On traces we tag spans with kv_cache=hit/miss so you can aggregate.
[02:39] Ava Chen: Note that the transcription might show KV 'cash' sometimes in other docs, that's just speech.
[02:45] Jordan Lee: Ha. Okay. For batching, we want queue wait time vs execution time breakdown at token granularity if possible.
[02:54] Samir Patel: We break request pipeline into these spans: host_queue_wait -> batch_assemble -> kernel_exec -> kv_cache_lookup -> token_decode. For token-level timing, token_decode and kernel_exec are per-token. We provide per-token histograms (bucketed) and also cumulative per-request.
[03:14] Ethan Brooks: Does quantization change kernel_exec time predictably? We saw mixed results with int8 vs int4 on our test infra.
[03:22] Samir Patel: Generally, more aggressive quantization reduces kernel execution time but sometimes increases decode overhead depending on the kernel. We emit quantization_profile as a label and also per-token kernel_exec_time. That lets you compare p50/p95 across profiles. Also if you use certain kernels, int4 can be slower at lower batch sizes due to vectorization inefficiencies.
[03:45] Priya Menon: For on-prem, sending OTLP out is a no-go for us. What's the private deployment path?
[03:52] Ava Chen: For Private deployments we can either run an OTLP collector inside your VPC that pushes to your observability backend, or you can point exporters directly at your internal collector. We support TLS mutual auth, OTLP/gRPC with certs and can integrate with your KMS for key rotation.
[04:10] Jordan Lee: Great. Can we run the collector sidecar on the same nodes as the inference runtime? Latency sensitive.
[04:17] Samir Patel: Yes, sidecar collector is common. We recommend buffering and batching before egress and using backpressure settings. Also consider rate limiting for spans to protect the runtime - we have config knobs to drop or sample high-cardinality spans under load.
[04:35] Ava Chen: Let's talk dashboards - what are the critical panels you want?
[04:39] Jordan Lee: Per-model p50/p95/p99 decode time, kernel exec time, queue wait time, batch size distribution, KV cache hit rate, request throughput, and cost-per-token if possible. Also example traces for p99 outliers.
[04:51] Samir Patel: Our Grafana template includes panels for per-token histogram heatmaps, batch size timeseries, cache hit ratio by shard, and a trace sample panel that links into the OTEL traces. We'll share the dashboard JSON.
[05:05] Ethan Brooks: For linking traces, is there a correlation ID we should propagate from our app?
[05:09] Samir Patel: Yes, propagate request_id. We also add model_request_id on the backend and return it in responses so you can stitch application traces and model traces.
[05:19] Priya Menon: Sampling strategy - what would you recommend for Atlas? We're heavy in telemetry already, might not want the volume.
[05:26] Samir Patel: Start with head-sampling: 1% of requests get full per-token spans, 100% metrics aggregated. Use rate-limited tail sampling for p99s - keep last N per minute. Also sample more for errors (status != OK) and cold starts. The collector can do tail-based sampling if you use an intermediary store or adaptive sampling controller.
[05:47] Jordan Lee: About cardinality - prompt_id hashed is fine. But we also want to attach customer_user_tier and feature_flag labels for routing cost analysis. Are those fine?
[05:57] Ava Chen: Those are fine as long as the label cardinality is bounded. If you have tens of tiers it's OK; if it's user_id scale it's not. For cost analysis, feature_flag and tier are common low-cardinality labels.
[06:10] Ethan Brooks: A practical question - how do we measure batching efficiency? Like, how often are we achieving intended batch_size?
[06:17] Samir Patel: We emit batch_size distribution, queued_request_count_over_time, and batching_efficiency = observed_tokens / theoretical_tokens. Also provide a batch_utilization gauge per worker. That lets you see the wasted slots.
[06:29] Priya Menon: If we run a pilot with a dedicated pool, can we get token-level traces without hitting our production telemetry quota?
[06:36] Samir Patel: Yes, run the pilot on a dedicated pool and either send OTLP to your dev telemetry project or to a local collector that you control. We can also sample heavily in the pilot to collect representative traces without full production volume.
[06:50] Jordan Lee: For security/compliance: are spans and metrics encrypted at rest and in-flight? Do they contain PII?
[06:58] Ava Chen: In hosted mode, telemetry is encrypted in transit with TLS and at rest with customer-specific keys where requested. We redact prompt text by default from labels and span attributes; prompt hashing option is recommended. For Private deployments, you control storage and retention. We'll share SOC2 artifacts and our telemetry handling docs.
[07:19] Ethan Brooks: There's mention of per-token 'queue wait' - how granular is that? Is it per-token or per-request?
[07:25] Samir Patel: Queue wait is measured at request enqueue time and at batch dispatch time; it's per-request. For per-token you can infer waiting if tokens are produced in waves, but token-level queue is typically the kernel_exec->token_decode timing.
[07:38] Jordan Lee: Could you walk through an example p99 trace and how we'd debug it?
[07:42] Samir Patel: Sure - sample trace: request_id -> host_queue_wait (120ms) -> batch_assemble (15ms) -> kernel_exec (p50 30ms, p99 500ms) -> kv_cache_lookup (if miss add 40ms) -> token_decode (per-token average 8ms). If p99 is 700ms, you'd look at kernel_exec spans for long tails, correlate with batch_size and shard_id, and check kv_cache misses. Also check model_variant label - maybe fallback to FP32 for some requests.
[08:18] Priya Menon: You mentioned fallback - is that for reliability? How is that recorded in telemetry?
[08:23] Samir Patel: Yes, fallback events are emitted as metrics fallback_count and also traced with a 'fallback_to_variant' attribute on the request span. That gives you counts and traces to investigate cause.
[08:36] Ava Chen: A note on wording: sometimes our docs say 'token-level metrics' vs 'per-token traces' - the former is aggregated histograms, the latter is full spans. We're recommending aggregated histograms for steady-state and sampled spans for debugging.
[08:50] Jordan Lee: For dashboards, if we want to show cost per token, how do we get cost data in? Does Redwood export cost attribution?
[08:58] Samir Patel: We export per-request token counts and model_variant cost coefficients. You can multiply tokens*coefficient in Grafana or push a derived metric. For Dedicated, we can provide a cost CSV mapping for your committed capacity.
[09:12] Ethan Brooks: Regarding quantization testing - can you instrument kernel-level counters to see mmapped memory usage and kernel stalls?
[09:20] Samir Patel: We expose runtime metrics like gpu_smem_usage_bytes, kernel_utilization_percent, and kernel_stall_cycles as gauges where our compilation layer supports it. That helps correlate kernel inefficiencies with quant profiles.
[09:34] Jordan Lee: Any pitfalls with OpenTelemetry versions or exporter settings we should watch?
[09:39] Samir Patel: Use OTLP gRPC exporter with compression for high volume. Avoid per-span synchronous exporters. Keep OTEL SDK up-to-date and align sampler configuration between SDK and collector. Watch collector resource limits - they can be a bottleneck if undersized.
[09:56] Priya Menon: On retention: we'd like to keep aggregated metrics for 90 days but traces for 30 days. Is that doable?
[10:03] Ava Chen: Yes, retention policies are typically on the telemetry backend. We can help with recommendations; in Private you control retention entirely. In hosted, we have options for tiered retention and archive.
[10:14] Jordan Lee: For the pilot, can you produce a dashboard that compares baseline (no cache, batch=1) vs optimized config (cache enabled, batch=8, int8) side-by-side?
[10:23] Samir Patel: Absolutely, that's a standard benchmark dashboard. We'll include comparative panels and heatmaps.
[10:29] Ethan Brooks: One last thing - do you provide a reference collector config for OTLP that includes tail-sampling rules?
[10:35] Samir Patel: Yes, we'll share a collector config with head and tail sampling snippets, plus instructions for backpressure and batching.
[10:42] Ava Chen: Awesome. Quick recap of next steps - we'll share docs and dashboards, you provide prompts and SLOs, then we schedule pilot. Any other questions?
[10:53] Jordan Lee: One minor nit - in our security review we will want to see proof of encryption keys and where they're stored; can you share KMS integrations?
[11:00] Ava Chen: Yes, we'll attach KMS integration docs in the follow-up.
[11:07] Priya Menon: Also send example RBAC policies for who can view traces vs metrics.
[11:13] Ava Chen: Noted.
[11:16] Ethan Brooks: Thanks, that's it from me.
[11:18] Ava Chen: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and scheduling.

End of call.
